extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, students and scholars of poetics/drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing tragic drama (plot, incidents, structure, and elements) to produce the proper tragic effect (pity and fear), drawn from Aristotle's Poetics. Focuses on unity, causality, reversal/discovery, characteral flaw, and staging/parts of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action
rubrics_metrics.description: 'a representation of a piece of action must represent a single piece of action and the whole of it; and the component incidents must be so arranged that if one of them be altered or removed, the unity of the whole is disturbed and destroyed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume unity simply because there is a single hero. Incidents must follow one another probably or inevitably (cause-and-effect); anything whose presence or absence makes no visible difference is not an integral part. Example: Homer did not record everything about Odysseus but constructed the Odyssey round a single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper magnitude (length) of the action
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the magnitude which admits of a change from bad fortune to good or from good fortune to bad, in a sequence of events which follow one another either inevitably or according to probability, that is the proper limit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer is better for magnitude provided the whole can be grasped at once. Magnitude should allow a single change of fortune to be represented coherently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must represent what could or would happen (probability/necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'a poet’s object is not to tell what actually happened but what could and would happen either probably or inevitably.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry aims at general truths about human types; plots should be constructed from probable or necessary chains of events rather than mere historical particulars. This distinguishes poetry from history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic plots
rubrics_metrics.description: 'episodic' = plots in which the episodes do not follow each other probably or inevitably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodic structure sacrifices continuity and unity, often written to please actors or competitions; such plots fail to produce the required tragic effect (fear and pity) because incidents appear accidental rather than causally linked. Good plotting exhibits cause-and-effect so incidents lead to one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce fear and pity by causal, surprising incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: the incidents should 'cause fear and pity... when the incidents are unexpected and yet one is a consequence of the other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best effects arise from incidents that surprise yet appear inevitable given prior events (not merely accidental). Providential-seeming coincidences are more moving than purely accidental occurrence (example: statue of Mytys).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex plot preferred to simple
rubrics_metrics.description: simple action: change of fortune occurs without reversal or discovery; complex action: change coincides with 'discovery' or 'reversal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots (those including reversal and/or discovery) are superior because they produce stronger moral/emotional effects. Structure should make the outcome inevitable or probable from prior events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'a reversal is a change of the situation into the opposite... this change being... probable or inevitable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal should be caused by the plot so that what has already happened leads to the opposite situation (example: Oedipus). Reversals are most effective when causally grounded and coincident with discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery (anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'a discovery... is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing either friendship or hatred... most effective when it coincides with reversals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery is most powerful when it transforms characters' relationships and is tied to the causal structure of the plot (example: the discovery in Oedipus). There are other, lesser forms of discovery (about inanimate facts, etc.), but the central form is interpersonal recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calamity as essential element
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A calamity is a destructive or painful occurrence, such as a death on the stage, acute suffering and wounding and so on.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Along with reversal and discovery, calamity (painful destructive events) is a core element of tragedy and often grounds pity/fear. The calamity should be appropriate to the plot's causal chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent parts of tragedy (structural ingredients)
rubrics_metrics.description: the separable members into which tragedy is quantitatively divided are: Prologue, Episode, Exode, Choral Song (Parode and Stasimon). A commos and songs sung by actors are peculiar to some plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: prologue = part before chorus entrance; episode = part between whole choral songs; exode = part not followed by a chorus song; parode = first utterance of chorus; stasimon = choral song without certain meters; commos = lament shared by chorus and actors. Use these parts appropriately when constructing a tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate moral complexion of tragic protagonist (mean character)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'one should not show worthy men passing from good fortune to bad... Nor again wicked people passing from bad fortune to good... There remains then the mean between these. This is the sort of man who is no paragon of virtue and righteousness... it is through some flaw of character... that he falls.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best tragic protagonists are neither wholly virtuous nor thoroughly vicious but high-status individuals who fall due to a significant character flaw (hamartia). This elicits both pity (undeserved misfortune) and fear (man like ourselves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single issue (single outcome) preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The successful plot must then have a single % and not, as some say, a double issue; and the change must be not to good fortune from bad but... from good to bad fortune.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a single outcome (unified dénouement) rather than a double ending (happiness for some, disaster for others). The change should be from good to bad to produce tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic effect should come from incidents, not spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the plot should be so constructed that even without seeing the play anyone hearing of the incidents happening thrills with fear and pity... To produce this effect by means of an appeal to the eye is inartistic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reliance on scenery, stage machinery, or grotesque spectacle to produce emotion; the arrangement of incidents (story) must generate pity and fear on its own. Visual 'monstrous' effects add little or are inartistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity/fear arise especially from calamities among close relations
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Such must necessarily be the actions of friends to each other or of enemies or of people that are neither... But when these calamities happen among friends, when for instance brother kills brother, or son father, or mother son... that is what we want.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents involving family or close relationships (kin-slaying, intended kin-slaying, betrayal among friends) are especially effective at arousing pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skillful use of tradition and invention
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the poet must show invention and make a skilful use of the tradition... It is not right to break up the traditional stories... but the poet must show invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not slavishly repeat traditional myths; instead adapt and invent within tradition so plot incidents remain plausible and artful. Tradition supplies material; skillful reshaping produces tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of ignorance/knowledge in committing tragic deeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Three alternatives for committing/avoiding an irremediable action: (a) intend action with full knowledge and not perform it (worst, 'outrages the feelings' since no calamity); (b) do the deed (less good); (c) act in ignorance and discover afterwards (better); (d) intend to do the deed in ignorance and discover before doing it (best — startling discovery, avoided deed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plots where characters act in ignorance and either discover afterwards (startling revelation) or, best, intend under ignorance and discover before acting (tension and reversal without gratuitous outrage). Avoid schemes where characters intend knowingly but abstain (no tragic calamity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause-and-effect (logical sequence) is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: 'what should result from the actual structure of the plot in such a way that what has already happened makes the result inevitable or probable... there is indeed a vast difference between what happens propter hoc and post hoc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange incidents so later events are consequences of earlier ones; the audience's sense of inevitability or probability strengthens the tragic effect. Avoid mere post hoc juxtapositions that lack causal grounding.
